title: Why should uploaded files NOT be stored on or streamed through the application server, how does a presigned URL let the client upload/download directly to object storage (S3/GCS) while your API only mints a short-lived signed URL, how do you upload a very large (multi-GB) file (S3 multipart upload in parts), and why must you validate the actual MIME type / magic bytes and enforce size limits rather than trusting the file extension (plus virus-scan untrusted user content)?
shortTitle: Why should uploaded files not be streamed through the application server, and how do presigned URLs, multipart upload, and MIME validation work

s1_definition.profdef: Routing file bytes through the application server couples your request threads, heap, and local disk to upload size and duration, which does not scale and risks OutOfMemoryError and disk exhaustion. A presigned URL is a time-limited, cryptographically signed URL generated by object storage (S3/GCS) that grants a client permission to perform one specific operation on one specific object, so the client transfers bytes directly to storage while your API only mints the URL. Multi-gigabyte uploads use multipart upload, splitting the object into independently uploaded parts that storage reassembles. You must verify the actual content type from the file's magic bytes rather than its extension, enforce a size limit, and virus-scan untrusted user content, because the extension and declared type are attacker-controlled and meaningless.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine every customer's heavy document box had to pass through the manager's own office. The manager's desk (heap) overflows, the office floor (disk) fills up, and the manager (thread) is stuck holding each box for the whole transfer. Instead the manager writes a one-time gate pass (presigned URL) that lets the customer drive straight to the warehouse (storage). For a truly enormous shipment, the customer splits it into labelled pallets (multipart) that the warehouse stacks back together. And the guard never trusts the label on the box; he opens it and checks what is actually inside (magic bytes) and scans it for anything dangerous (virus scan) before it is accepted.
s1_definition.oneliner: The app server mints a short-lived signed URL and steps aside; bytes go client-to-storage directly, in parts if huge, and you trust the file's actual contents, never its label.

**Professional definition:** Routing file bytes through the application server couples your request threads, heap, and local disk to upload size and duration, which does not scale and risks OutOfMemoryError and disk exhaustion. A presigned URL is a time-limited, cryptographically signed URL generated by object storage (S3/GCS) that grants a client permission to perform one specific operation on one specific object, so the client transfers bytes directly to storage while your API only mints the URL. Multi-gigabyte uploads use multipart upload, splitting the object into independently uploaded parts that storage reassembles. You must verify the actual content type from the file's magic bytes rather than its extension, enforce a size limit, and virus-scan untrusted user content, because the extension and declared type are attacker-controlled and meaningless.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine every customer's heavy document box had to pass through the manager's own office. The manager's desk (heap) overflows, the office floor (disk) fills up, and the manager (thread) is stuck holding each box for the whole transfer. Instead the manager writes a one-time gate pass (presigned URL) that lets the customer drive straight to the warehouse (storage). For a truly enormous shipment, the customer splits it into labelled pallets (multipart) that the warehouse stacks back together. And the guard never trusts the label on the box; he opens it and checks what is actually inside (magic bytes) and scans it for anything dangerous (virus scan) before it is accepted.

**One line to remember:** The app server mints a short-lived signed URL and steps aside; bytes go client-to-storage directly, in parts if huge, and you trust the file's actual contents, never its label.

sections.s2_technical:
Why not stream through the app server. Three resources get consumed per upload when bytes pass through your service: heap memory if you buffer, a request thread for the entire upload duration, and local disk if you spool to temp files. A single slow 2 GB upload on a mobile connection can hold a thread for ten minutes. A few hundred concurrent large uploads exhaust the thread pool, blow the heap, or fill the disk, and your service falls over even though it is doing no useful computation, just copying bytes. Your application server should spend its CPU and threads on business logic, not on being a dumb byte pipe that object storage does far better and cheaper.

How a presigned URL works. Object storage like S3 lets an authorized backend generate a URL that embeds a signature computed from your secret credentials, the target bucket and key, the allowed HTTP method, and an expiry time. Anyone holding that URL can perform exactly that one operation until it expires, without any credentials of their own. The flow: the client asks your API to upload a file; your API authenticates the user, validates the request, and calls the S3 presigner to produce a PUT URL for a specific key valid for a few minutes; the client uploads the bytes straight to S3 with that URL; S3 verifies the signature and stores the object. For downloads you mint a GET URL the same way. Your API handles only tiny JSON, never the file. In code the generation is `s3Presigner.presignPutObject(req -> req.signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).putObjectRequest(por))` which returns the signed URL string.

How multi-gigabyte multipart upload works. A single PUT is impractical for very large files because a network blip restarts the whole transfer. S3 multipart upload breaks the object into parts, typically 5 MB to 100 MB each. The flow is: initiate a multipart upload and get an upload ID; for each part, the client (via a presigned URL per part) uploads that chunk and receives an ETag; after all parts are uploaded, the client calls complete with the list of part numbers and ETags, and S3 assembles the final object. Parts upload in parallel for speed, a failed part retries alone, and you can abort to clean up incomplete uploads. This gives resumability, parallelism, and bounded memory per part.

Why you must validate actual MIME type and size, not the extension. The file extension and the client-declared Content-Type are attacker-controlled strings. An attacker renames malware.exe to invoice.pdf and sets Content-Type to application/pdf. If you trust that, you store and later serve an executable as a PDF. The reliable check is the magic bytes, the first few bytes of the file that identify the real format: a PDF starts with the bytes for "%PDF", a PNG starts with a specific 8-byte signature, a JPEG with FF D8 FF. You read the leading bytes and verify they match an allowed type. Libraries like Apache Tika do this detection robustly. You also enforce a hard maximum size before issuing a URL and, for multipart, cap total size, so nobody uploads a 500 GB file to exhaust your storage budget or trigger a cost attack.

Why virus-scan untrusted content. Users upload arbitrary bytes. Those bytes may be malware, and if your system later serves them to other users or opens them in a processing pipeline, you spread infection. So uploaded content lands in a quarantine area, an asynchronous scanner such as ClamAV checks it, and only clean files are promoted to the usable bucket. Infected files are rejected and the user notified. Scanning is asynchronous so it never blocks the upload path.

The senior nuance is that signed URLs must be short-lived and tightly scoped. A URL valid for days or for a whole bucket is a leaked-credential waiting to happen. You scope it to one key, one method, a short expiry, and ideally with a content-length-range and content-type condition so the client cannot upload something other than what you authorized.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India accepts loan documents and KYC videos from customers like Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001). Some are 3 GB scanned archives.

Problem 1 — the app server fell over as a byte pipe. The old design streamed every upload through the service to disk, then to S3. During a loan drive the disk filled and the thread pool drained while the CPU sat idle, because the server was just copying bytes. This is why we mint a presigned URL and let the client upload straight to S3: the server stops being a byte pipe.

Problem 2 — a 3 GB upload kept failing near the end and restarting from zero. A single PUT over a flaky connection never completed. This is why multi-gigabyte files use multipart upload: the file is split into parts, each uploaded and retried independently, and only the failed part is re-sent.

Problem 3 — an attacker uploaded a program renamed to statement.pdf. The old system trusted the .pdf extension and stored it. This is why we verify magic bytes (a real PDF begins with %PDF), enforce a size cap, and virus-scan in quarantine before promoting the file.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the control logic: a `PresignService` that mints scoped short-lived URLs, a `MultipartCoordinator` that initiates, tracks parts, and completes a multi-GB upload, a `MagicByteValidator` that checks real file type, a size guard, and a `QuarantineScanner`. It presigns Rajesh's single PDF, runs Priya's 3 GB multipart upload, and rejects a spoofed file.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/secure-upload-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.secureupload.SecureUploadDemo

# Single presigned PUT
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/uploads/presign \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"userId":"SAV2001","filename":"loan_form.pdf","sizeBytes":20971520}'

# Multipart: initiate, then upload each part to its own presigned URL, then complete
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/uploads/multipart/initiate \
  -d '{"userId":"CUR3001","filename":"kyc_video.mp4","sizeBytes":3221225472}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's 20 MB PDF, Priya's 3 GB video, a spoofed EXE named statement.pdf, and a genuine PDF.

Step 1: Rajesh's 20 MB is under the 100 MB single-PUT limit, so SizeGuard passes it. PresignService mints a PUT URL for key SAV2001/loan_form.pdf valid five minutes. Rajesh uploads the bytes directly to S3; the server never sees them.

Step 2: Priya's 3 GB exceeds the single-PUT limit, so it goes multipart. The coordinator initiates and gets an upload ID. planParts divides 3 GB by 16 MB parts, giving 192 parts.

Step 3: For each part the coordinator mints a per-part presigned URL. Priya's client uploads each 16 MB chunk directly to S3 and collects an ETag per part. A failed part retries alone, not the whole 3 GB.

Step 4: After all 192 parts are in, complete is called with the part numbers and ETags, and S3 assembles the final object. Priya's video exists as one object.

Step 5: The spoofed file arrives with extension .pdf and declared type application/pdf, but its first bytes are MZ, the DOS executable header. MagicByteValidator detects application/x-dosexec, which is not in the allowed set, and throws UnsupportedFileTypeException. The spoof is rejected regardless of its fake label.

Step 6: The genuine PDF begins with %PDF, so the validator detects application/pdf and passes it. It lands in quarantine, the scanner checks it, returns CLEAN, and it is promoted to the clean bucket for use.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Rajesh single-PUT presigned URL: https://nbi-uploads-raw.s3.amazonaws.com/SAV2001/loan_form.pdf?...
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Priya multipart initiated id=UP-7c2a... parts=192
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] COMPLETE multipart UP-7c2a... with 192 parts → S3 assembles object
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [SEVERE ] SPOOF REJECTED: declared=application/pdf but magic bytes say=application/x-dosexec for statement.pdf
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Rajesh file scan result: CLEAN → promoted from quarantine to clean bucket
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I do not route uploaded file bytes through my application server because doing so couples three scarce resources to the size and duration of every upload: heap memory if I buffer, a request thread held for the entire transfer, and local disk if I spool to temp files. A single slow multi-gigabyte upload on a mobile connection can hold a thread for ten minutes, and a few hundred concurrent large uploads exhaust the thread pool, blow the heap, or fill the disk, while the CPU sits idle because the server is doing no real work, just copying bytes. The application server should spend its threads on business logic, not on being a dumb byte pipe that object storage does far better and cheaper.

Instead I use presigned URLs. Object storage like S3 can generate a URL that embeds a signature derived from my backend credentials, the specific bucket and key, the allowed method, and a short expiry. The client asks my API to upload, I authenticate and validate the request and mint a PUT URL valid for a few minutes, and the client then uploads the bytes directly to S3 using that URL while my API only ever handles tiny JSON. For downloads I mint a GET URL the same way. The key safety rule is that the URL must be short-lived and tightly scoped to one key and one operation, ideally with a content-length-range condition, so a leaked URL expires quickly and cannot be abused.

For multi-gigabyte files a single PUT is impractical because any network blip restarts the whole transfer, so I use S3 multipart upload. I initiate and get an upload ID, the client uploads each part through its own presigned URL and collects an ETag per part, parts upload in parallel and a failed part retries on its own, and finally a complete call with the list of part numbers and ETags tells S3 to assemble the object. This gives me parallelism, resumability, and bounded memory per part, which is exactly how we fixed Priya's 3 GB KYC video that previously failed near the end and restarted from zero.

On validation, I never trust the file extension or the client-declared content type, because both are attacker-controlled strings. An attacker renames an executable to statement.pdf and claims it is a PDF. So I read the file's magic bytes, the leading signature that identifies the real format, where a PDF begins with the bytes for percent-P-D-F and an executable begins with MZ, and I reject anything whose real type is not in my allow-list. I enforce a hard maximum size before issuing any URL so nobody can trigger a storage or cost attack, and because users upload arbitrary untrusted bytes, uploaded content lands in a quarantine bucket where an asynchronous scanner like ClamAV checks it, and only clean files are promoted to the usable bucket while infected files are deleted and the user alerted.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that my API mints a short-lived, scoped, signed URL and then steps aside, so bytes travel directly from the client to object storage, very large files go up as independently retryable multipart chunks, and I trust the file's actual magic bytes and enforce a size cap and a quarantine virus scan rather than ever trusting its extension or declared type.
